Methods: Thirty-eight healthy volunteers with a mean age of
28 years participated. Surface recording electrodes were used. The
active electrode was located on the middle of the line connecting
the midpopliteal fossa with the medial malleolus. The reference elec-
trodes were located in three different points: the distal portion of the
achilles tendon, the midpoint of the aponeurosis on the gastocnem-
ius muscle, and the point aponeurosis adjoining the two heads of the
gastrocnemius muscle. The ground electrode was positioned on the
midpoint of the stimulation point and the active electrode. The M-
wave amplitude and H-wave amplitude, latency, and shape were
measured. Statistical analyses were performed with ANOVA by SPSS
software.
Results: The M-wave amplitude was the lowest at the third loca-
tion in both sides. Locations one and two showed no difference be-
tween each other. The H-wave amplitude was the highest at
location two in both sides. Locations one and three showed no differ-
ence between each other. The H-wave latency revealed no difference
between the three locations. All H-waves from the three reference
locations showed initial negative two phasic morphology.
Conclusion: By locating the reference electrode to the midpoint
of the gastrocnemius aponeurosis, it was possible to generate higher
H-wave amplitude without changing other measures.

116. Stiff person syndrome improvement with chemotherapy
in a patient with cutaneous T cell lymphoma—G. Rakocevic,
A. Hussain (Philadelphia, PA, USA)
Introduction: Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is usually idiopathic,
but it can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of certain tumors, most
commonly secondary to breast adenocarcinoma and small cell lung
cancer and associated with anti-amphiphysin antibodies. In both
cases there is impaired synaptic gamma-aminobutyric acid
(GABA)-ergic neurotransmission resulting from autoantibodies tar-
geting various presynaptic and synaptic proteins in the inhibitory
neurons of the brain and spinal cord.
Objectives: The authors describe a patient with glutamic acid
decarboxylase antibodies (anti-GAD) positive and amphiphysin neg-
ative antibody SPS and long-standing cutaneous T cell lymphoma
treated successfully with multiple courses of T cell- and B cell-
depleting monoclonal antibodies with near-resolution of her SPS
symptoms.
Methods: The patient is a 57-year-old woman diagnosed with T
cell lymphoma at age 40 years, who underwent initial cytoxan treat-
ments followed by intermittent rituximab infusions. She was diag-
nosed with GAD-positive SPS at age 46 years and treated with oral
steroids and intermittent plasma exchanges without beneﬁt.
Results: The patient’s lymphoma exacerbations have been associ-
ated with worsening of SPS in general. In addition to intermittent rit-
uximab infusions for lymphoma relapses and as a maintenance
therapy over years, she has also received alemtuzumab, bexarotene,
tacrolimus, and azathioprine on separate occasions with a dramatic
improvement of truncal stiffness and gait stability. Intravenous
immunoglobulin (IVIg) was given for chemotherapy-induced hypo-
gammaglobulinemia and frequent sinusitis and respiratory infec-
tions, with near-resolution of SPS-related painful muscle spasms.
Conclusion: SPS symptoms beneﬁt from T and B cell-targeted
therapies. Early detection and the treatment of primary cancer asso-
ciated with sporadic or paraneoplastic SPS are crucial for a patient’s

survival and neurological outcome.
doi:10.1016/j.clinph.2011.11.198
117. Superﬁcial radial sensory neuropathy: Medial and lateral
branch injuries—D.H. Kim (Ansan, Gyeonggi Province, South
Korea)
Introduction: The superﬁcial radial sensory nerve (SRN) bifur-
cates into the medial and lateral branches around the distal forearm
and may be injured either at the main trunk or the isolated medial or
lateral branches by various etiologies.
Objectives: To demonstrate the usefulness of superﬁcial radial
sensory nerve conduction studies (SR-SNCSs) for the medial and lat-
eral branches of the SRN in 15 patients with superﬁcial radial sen-
sory neuropathy.
Methods: Fifteen patients (3 women, 12 men; median age,
39 years; range, 19–49 years) with symptoms of superﬁcial radial
sensory neuropathy were evaluated with SR-SNCSs that consisted
of three active recording electrode positions (the base of the snuff
box, the extensor pollicis longus tendon at the medial branch cross-
ing point; and just lateral to the abductor pollicis longus and exten-
sor pollicis brevis tendons), which was recently published
Results: All patients had traumatic causes: 8 radius or ulanr frac-
tures, 5 lacerations, and 2 operations for De Quervain’s disease.
There were isolated injuries of the medial (8) and lateral branches
(5) of the SRN. Injury of both branches was due to deep laceration
on the forearm. The sensory symptom area was consistent with elec-
trophysiologic ﬁndings of the branches of the SRN.
Conclusion: SR-SNCSs for the medial and lateral branches of the
SRN are useful for evaluating superﬁcial radial sensory neuro-
pathy, especially isolated medial or lateral branch injury of the
SRN.

118. The value of free run needle electromyography monitoring
of cranial nerve V during endoscopic endonasal approach to skull
base surgery—M.R. Potter, P.D. Thirumala, D.J. Crammond,
P. Gardner, M. Habeych, J. Balzer, C. Snyderman (Pittsburgh, PA,
USA)
Introduction: The use of intraoperative neurophysiological mon-
itoring (IONM), speciﬁcally free run needle electromyography (f-
EMG), has been used to identify and prevent cranial nerve (CN)
deﬁcits.
Objectives: The authors will evaluate the value of f-EMG from CN
V during endoscopic endonasal approach (EEA) surgery. EEA surgery
is a minimally invasive form of skull base surgery. To date, no studies
have been conducted examining the value of f-EMG of CN V during
skull base surgeries and/or EEA.
Methods: Seventeen patients were examined who had f-EMG
monitoring on CN V during EEA surgery. A total of 27 CN V nerves
were monitored among all of the patients. Of those 17 patients, some
received additional nerve monitoring on CNs VII, IX, X, XI, and XII
taking the total number of nerves observed to 91.
Results: One patient had signiﬁcant f-EMG activity during the
case and did not have any neurological deﬁcits. Of the other cranial
nerves monitored signiﬁcant f-EMG activity was present in CNs VII,
IX, X in 14%, 12%, 21% of all nerves monitored, respectively. No pa-
tients had postoperative neurological deﬁcits.
Conclusion: Through f-EMG monitoring of the trigeminal nerve
during EEA surgery, surgeons are able to identify the location of
the nerve and prevent deﬁcits by observing the nerve’s activity.
